makefileSection.title: Introduction to Makefiles
makefileSection.content: One of the tools that can help automate the compilation process and simplify working with larger projects is Makefiles. A Makefile is a file used by the 'make' utility to automate the building (compiling and linking) of programs. It contains rules and instructions on how to compile and link the different parts of a program. In large projects, where you have many .c files, Makefiles help ensure that only the necessary files are recompiled when changes are made. This saves time and prevents unnecessary recompilation.

makefileParts.variables: Variables are used to store values like compiler flags or file names.
makefileParts.rules: Rules define how files should be compiled. Each rule has a target (the file to be built), dependencies (files that are needed for the target), and the command to build the target.
makefileParts.commands: Commands are the specific shell commands that the Makefile will run when it executes the rule.

example.makefile:
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -std=c99 -Wall

all: program

program: program.o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) program.o -o program

program.o: program.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c program.c

clean:
	rm -f *.o program

explanation.CFLAGS: Compiler flags (-std=c99 ensures the use of the C99 standard, and -Wall enables all warnings).
explanation.all: The default target that will be built when you run make. It depends on the program target.
explanation.program: This target depends on program.o, and the command to build it is gcc program.o -o program.
explanation.clean: A special target that removes all object files and the executable. You can run this with make clean to clean up the directory.

makefileBenefits.title: Why Use Makefiles?
content: Using Makefiles is beneficial for several reasons:
1. Automation: It automates the compilation process, saving you from having to type out long commands every time you need to compile your program.
2. Efficiency: 'make' will only recompile the files that have changed, instead of recompiling the entire program. This is especially useful for larger projects.
3. Consistency: Makefiles provide a standardized way to manage the build process across different machines and developers.

bestPractices.title: Makefile Best Practices
content: 1. Use Variables: Variables make your Makefile more flexible and easier to maintain.
2. Modularize Your Project: If your project grows large, break it up into multiple subdirectories and use Makefiles in each subdirectory.
3. Use Dependencies Wisely: Make sure the dependencies are correctly set to avoid unnecessary recompilation.
